<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion. PRO held the decisive burden frame — the motion stipulates the screen does not drive performance, so CON had to defend a criterion it conceded was not job-related — and then answered CON's strongest move (the "vacuum": drop the degree and screening goes underground toward referrals and gut feel) with a concrete, posted, connection-independent "broadened floor" (degree OR relevant work OR apprenticeship OR military service). CON's reply that this is merely the status quo shows the motion may be modest, but modesty is not a harm, and CON never showed the broadened floor is less open than degree-only. PRO also converted CON's own "hiring barely changed" evidence into a costlessness point and landed the best weighing of the debate: if PRO is wrong employers read a few more applications; if CON is wrong capable workers are locked out to save a manager an afternoon. PRO's closing turn — that "capacity is fixed" only works if the fifty résumés must be cut by something arbitrary, making CON a defense of convenience rather than standards — was the cleanest crystallization on the table. CON's transparency argument ("the only gate with a published price," a rule she can see and earn) was original, well-executed, and kept the debate close, and CON answered the "who decides" and litigation-exposure lines competently. But CON's route depended on the added routes being less legible than a diploma, which PRO specified against and CON did not squarely refute. CON also absorbed an extra clipping cost on Rebuttal 2.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's handling of CON's fixed-capacity/vacuum argument: first specifying a posted, connectionless broadened floor that cuts the same pile at no extra employer cost, then reframing "capacity is fixed" in closing as an admission that the first cut is arbitrary — turning CON's central mechanism into a defense of hiring convenience rather than standards.</best_rebuttal>
